\chapter{Understanding, Reading, Writing}
\label{ch:ar-understanding-reading-writing}
\hlchaptermodality{31}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say the Arabic for 'he understood', 'he read', 'he asked' and 'he wrote', and build a whole family of nouns off each root using the doer, done-to and ma- place shapes I already know.}

Run \ar{ك}-\ar{ت}-\ar{ب} through every pattern the track has taught — kitāb, kātib, maktūb, maktab, maktaba — naming the earlier word that wears each shape (qāʾil and qāriʾ for the doer, maqūl and mafhūm and maqrūʾ for the done-to, madhhab and masʾala for the ma- place), then place the root beside Hebrew katav and English ketubah.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[fahima]{\ar{فهم} (fahima) — \textquotedblleft{}he understood,\textquotedblright{} and the vowel that makes a state}

\label{lesson:AR-C31-fahima}



\begin{quote}
Six verbs so far, every one of them a deed. This one is not: it happens inside a person — and Arabic marks that in the vowels.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Nothing new in \textbf{\ar{فهم}} itself: \textbf{\ar{ف}} (\emph{fāʾ}, one dot), \textbf{\ar{ه}} (\emph{hāʾ}) and \textbf{\ar{م}} (\emph{mīm}), with \emph{fāʾ}'s two-dotted partner \textbf{\ar{ق}} the pair sorted out in \emph{ʿarafa}. That is twice running — \textbf{\ar{أكل}} needed no new letters either.

One letter does need naming, because every word-family ahead reaches for it: \textbf{\ar{و}} (\emph{wāw}). You have read it unnamed inside \textbf{\ar{قَوْل}} (\emph{qawl}), \textquotedblleft{}a saying.\textquotedblright{} It is a \textbf{non-joiner}, a small loop with a tail under the line, and it holds two jobs — the consonant \emph{w}, and the long vowel \textbf{ū}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{فَهِمَ}} (\emph{fahima}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{he understood}.\textquotedblright{} Root \textbf{\ar{ف}-\ar{ه}-\ar{م}}.

Listen to the middle vowel. \emph{Dhahaba}, \emph{qāla}, \emph{ʿarafa} and \emph{akala} all ran \emph{a-a-a}, the \textbf{\ar{فَعَلَ}} (\emph{faʿala}) shape. \emph{Fahima} runs \emph{a-i-a}: \textbf{\ar{فَعِلَ}} (\emph{faʿila}), which Arabic keeps for \textbf{states} rather than deeds. Understanding is not performed; it arrives.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{فَهْم}} (\emph{fahm}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{understanding},\textquotedblright{} the bare thing.
  \item \textbf{\ar{مَفْهوم}} (\emph{mafhūm}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{understood},\textquotedblright{} the \textbf{done-to} shape of \emph{mashkūr} and \emph{maqūl}, its long \emph{ū} riding that \textbf{\ar{و}}. As a noun it is \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a concept}\textquotedblright{}: a thing that has been understood.
\end{itemize}

And the flat statement \emph{akala} insisted on holds here too: \textbf{\ar{ف}-\ar{ه}-\ar{م} has no English relative.} \emph{Fathom} is Germanic; the resemblance is noise. No Hebrew twin worth the claim, either.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item two words needing no new letters — akala, then fahima
  \item the two shapes — akala, a-a-a; fahima, a-i-a
  \item \textquotedblleft{}fahima,\textquotedblright{} he understood — then fahm, understanding; mafhūm, a concept
  \item the dots once more — \ar{ف} one, \ar{ق} two, one body between them
  \item three roots, three ideas — maʿrifa, knowledge; fahm, understanding; akl, food
  \item the honest line — no English cousin here, as with akala
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which vowel of \emph{fahima} differs from \emph{akala}, and what does it mark? (\textbf{The middle \emph{i}} — \textbf{\ar{فَعِلَ}}, a state rather than a deed.) What is \textbf{\ar{مَفْهوم}}? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Understood,\textquotedblright{} and so \textquotedblleft{}a concept\textquotedblright{}} — the done-to shape of \emph{maqūl} and \emph{mashkūr}.) Does \emph{fahima} have an English cousin? (\textbf{No} — \emph{fathom} is Germanic.) Which letter was named here, and where had you read it? (\textbf{\ar{و}}, \emph{wāw} — inside \emph{qawl}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[qaraʾa]{\ar{قرأ} (qaraʾa) — \textquotedblleft{}he recited,\textquotedblright{} and the word English spells Quran}

\label{lesson:AR-C31-qaraa}



\begin{quote}
One root in this chapter did give English a word — exactly one, and it is not the word for reading.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ar{ق}} (\emph{qāf}, two dots) and \textbf{\ar{ر}} (\emph{rāʾ}) are yours. The third is \textbf{\ar{أ}}, \emph{hamza} on an \emph{alif} seat, closing the word.

Hamza is the homeless consonant. It has a sound of its own — the catch in \textquotedblleft{}uh-oh\textquotedblright{} — but usually no letter, so it borrows a \textbf{seat}, and which seat depends on the vowels around it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{أ}} — hamza on \textbf{\ar{ا}}, as in \textbf{\ar{قَرَأَ}} and in \textbf{\ar{أنت}}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{ؤ}} — hamza on \textbf{\ar{و}}, the letter named last lesson.
  \item \textbf{\ar{ئ}} — hamza on \textbf{\ar{ي}}, which gives up its dots to carry it.
  \item \textbf{\ar{ء}} — and where no seat suits, hamza alone on the line, closing \textbf{\ar{جاء}}.
\end{itemize}

Four spellings, one consonant. The seat is bookkeeping; the hamza is the sound.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{قَرَأَ}} (\emph{qaraʾa}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{he read}\textquotedblright{} — nearer the root's heart, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{he recited aloud}.\textquotedblright{} Reading here is done with the voice. Root \textbf{\ar{ق}-\ar{ر}-\ar{أ}}, plain \emph{faʿala} shape.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{قارِئ}} (\emph{qāriʾ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a \textbf{reader},\textquotedblright{} the \textbf{doer} shape of \emph{qāʾil}, hamza on its dotless \emph{yāʾ} seat.
  \item \textbf{\ar{مَقْروء}} (\emph{maqrūʾ}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{read},\textquotedblright{} the \textbf{done-to} shape of \emph{mafhūm}, long \emph{ū} on the \textbf{\ar{و}}, hamza left seatless at the end.
  \item \textbf{\ar{قُرْآن}} (\emph{qurʾān}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the recitation},\textquotedblright{} the thing recited. English writes it \textbf{Quran}, or \textbf{Koran}. Its long \textbf{\ar{آ}} is the alif-and-hamza fusion already met in \textbf{\ar{آكِل}} (\emph{ākil}), \textquotedblleft{}an eater.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

That single loan is the shape of the whole story. Arabic gave English \emph{algebra}, \emph{alcohol}, \emph{coffee}, \emph{sugar} and \emph{admiral} — goods and sciences, nouns nearly every one. Out of \textbf{\ar{ق}-\ar{ر}-\ar{أ}} travelled not \textquotedblleft{}to read\textquotedblright{} but the name of a book. The nearer relative is Hebrew \textbf{\he{קָרָא}} (\emph{qara}), \textquotedblleft{}he read.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item hamza's seats — \ar{أ} on alif, \ar{ؤ} on wāw, \ar{ئ} on dotless yāʾ, \ar{ء} on nothing
  \item \textquotedblleft{}qaraʾa,\textquotedblright{} he recited — then qāriʾ, a reader
  \item the done-to pair — mafhūm, a concept; maqrūʾ, read — both on wāw
  \item the borrowed word — qurʾān, \textquotedblleft{}the recitation,\textquotedblright{} English Quran
  \item the fused alif — ākil, an eater; qurʾān
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which three seats can hamza take, and what happens to the \emph{yāʾ} when it serves? (\textbf{\ar{ا}, \ar{و} and \ar{ي}} — the \emph{yāʾ} \textbf{drops its dots}: \ar{ئ}.) Which English word descends from \textbf{\ar{ق}-\ar{ر}-\ar{أ}}, and what does it mean in Arabic? (\textbf{Quran} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the recitation}.\textquotedblright{}) Which letter carries the long \emph{ū} of \textbf{\ar{مَقْروء}}? (\textbf{\ar{و}}.) Which earlier word shares the fused \textbf{\ar{آ}}? (\textbf{\ar{آكِل}}, \emph{ākil}, \textquotedblleft{}an eater.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[saʾala]{\ar{سأل} (saʾala) — \textquotedblleft{}he asked,\textquotedblright{} and the Arabic word for answerable}

\label{lesson:AR-C31-saala}



\begin{quote}
Hamza sat at the end of the last word. Here it sits in the middle — and as the vowels shift around it, it changes seats without changing sound at all.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Nothing new: \textbf{\ar{س}} (\emph{sīn}), \textbf{\ar{أ}} (hamza on its \emph{alif} seat) and \textbf{\ar{ل}} (\emph{lām}). Right to left, \emph{sa-ʾa-la}.

What is worth doing is watching that seat move while the root holds still:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{سَأَلَ}} (\emph{saʾala}) — the \emph{a} keeps hamza on \textbf{\ar{ا}}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{سُؤال}} (\emph{suʾāl}) — the \emph{u} pulls it onto \textbf{\ar{و}}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{سائِل}} (\emph{sāʾil}) — the \emph{i} pulls it onto dotless \textbf{\ar{ي}}.
\end{itemize}

One consonant, one root, three spellings — exactly the rule laid out with \emph{qaraʾa}, now doing its work inside a single family.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{سَأَلَ}} (\emph{saʾala}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{he asked}.\textquotedblright{} Root \textbf{\ar{س}-\ar{أ}-\ar{ل}}, the plain \emph{faʿala} shape.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{سُؤال}} (\emph{suʾāl}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a question}.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{\ar{سائِل}} (\emph{sāʾil}) — \textquotedblleft{}an \textbf{asker},\textquotedblright{} the doer shape that also gave \emph{qāriʾ}, \textquotedblleft{}a reader.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{\ar{مَسْأَلة}} (\emph{masʾala}) — the \emph{\textbf{ma-}} shape: \textquotedblleft{}a \textbf{matter}, a \textbf{problem}\textquotedblright{} — a thing asked about.
  \item \textbf{\ar{مَسْؤول}} (\emph{masʾūl}) — the \textbf{done-to} shape, literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{asked-of},\textquotedblright{} and so \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{responsible}\textquotedblright{}; as a noun, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{an official}.\textquotedblright{} Arabic builds accountability out of being the one who gets questioned, which is a fair account of what accountability is.
\end{itemize}

The Hebrew twin is exact: \textbf{\he{שָׁאַל}} (\emph{shaʾal}), \textquotedblleft{}he asked\textquotedblright{} — Arabic \emph{s} against Hebrew \emph{sh}, the same swap heard between \emph{salām} and \emph{shalom}. Its passive participle is the name \textbf{\he{שָׁאוּל}} (\emph{Shaʾul}), English \textbf{Saul}: \textquotedblleft{}asked for.\textquotedblright{} From the Arabic root, English took nothing.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the seat moving — saʾala on alif, suʾāl on wāw, sāʾil on dotless yāʾ
  \item \textquotedblleft{}saʾala\textquotedblright{} — he asked — then suʾāl, a question
  \item the two doers — qāriʾ, a reader; sāʾil, an asker
  \item masʾala, a matter — masʾūl, asked-of, and so responsible
  \item the twins — Arabic saʾala, Hebrew shaʾal, and the name Saul
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which three seats does hamza take across \emph{saʾala}, \emph{suʾāl} and \emph{sāʾil}? (\textbf{Alif, wāw, dotless yāʾ} — one consonant, three spellings.) What does \textbf{\ar{مَسْؤول}} mean literally, and what does it mean in use? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Asked-of\textquotedblright{}} — and so \textbf{responsible}, or an official.) Which two words here wear the doer shape? (\emph{\textbf{Sāʾil}}, an asker, and \emph{\textbf{qāriʾ}}, a reader.) What does the name \textbf{Saul} mean? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Asked for\textquotedblright{}} — from Hebrew \emph{shaʾal}, twin of \textbf{\ar{سَأَلَ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kataba]{\ar{كتب} (kataba) — \textquotedblleft{}he wrote,\textquotedblright{} and the root that furnishes a library}

\label{lesson:AR-C31-kataba}



\begin{quote}
The chapter closes on the root every Arabic grammar reaches for first. Three letters — and you already own every pattern they need.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ar{ك}} (\emph{kāf}), \textbf{\ar{ت}} (\emph{tāʾ}, two dots) and \textbf{\ar{ب}} (\emph{bāʾ}, one dot below) were taught long ago. New is how they sit together: \textbf{all three join}, so \textbf{\ar{كتب}} is one unbroken run of pen — unlike \textbf{\ar{ذهب}}, where \emph{dhāl} refuses to connect, or \textbf{\ar{أكل}}, where the \emph{alif} stands off alone.

One old mark earns its keep too: put \textbf{\ar{ة}} (\emph{tāʾ marbūṭa}) on \textbf{\ar{مَكْتَب}} (\emph{maktab}) and you get \textbf{\ar{مَكْتَبة}} (\emph{maktaba}). One letter, and an office becomes a library.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{كَتَبَ}} (\emph{kataba}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{he wrote}.\textquotedblright{} Root \textbf{\ar{ك}-\ar{ت}-\ar{ب}}, plain \emph{faʿala} shape. Now pour it through the patterns this track has handed you:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{كِتاب}} (\emph{kitāb}) — \textquotedblleft{}a \textbf{book}.\textquotedblright{} A written thing.
  \item \textbf{\ar{كاتِب}} (\emph{kātib}) — \textquotedblleft{}a \textbf{writer},\textquotedblright{} the \textbf{doer} shape of \emph{qāʾil} and \emph{qāriʾ}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{مَكْتوب}} (\emph{maktūb}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{written},\textquotedblright{} the \textbf{done-to} shape of \emph{maqūl} and \emph{mafhūm} — and in speech, what has been written for you: \textbf{fate}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{مَكْتَب}} (\emph{maktab}) — the \emph{\textbf{ma-}} \textbf{place} shape of \emph{madhhab} and \emph{masjid}: the place of writing, a \textbf{desk}, an \textbf{office}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{مَكْتَبة}} (\emph{maktaba}) — that place plus \textbf{\ar{ة}}: a \textbf{library}.
\end{itemize}

Five words off one root, not one of them learned separately. That is the whole return on the root system, collected in one lesson.

No English word descends from \textbf{\ar{ك}-\ar{ت}-\ar{ب}}. English does hold one from the same \textbf{Semitic} root, by way of Hebrew: a \textbf{ketubah}, the written Jewish marriage contract — \textbf{\he{כְּתוּבָּה}} (\emph{ketubbah}), \textquotedblleft{}a written thing,\textquotedblright{} from \textbf{\he{כָּתַב}} (\emph{katav}), \textquotedblleft{}he wrote.\textquotedblright{} That is \emph{maktūb}'s own pattern in the other language.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item three joined letters — kāf, tāʾ, bāʾ — \textquotedblleft{}kataba,\textquotedblright{} he wrote
  \item the doers — qāʾil, qāriʾ, kātib
  \item the done-to run — maqūl, mafhūm, maqrūʾ, maktūb
  \item the ma- place shape — madhhab, masʾala, maktab
  \item the letter that moves — maktab, an office; maktaba, a library
  \item the Semitic twin — Hebrew katav, English ketubah
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name five words built here from \textbf{\ar{ك}-\ar{ت}-\ar{ب}}. (\emph{\textbf{Kitāb}}, \emph{\textbf{kātib}}, \emph{\textbf{maktūb}}, \emph{\textbf{maktab}}, \emph{\textbf{maktaba}}.) Which pattern gives \textquotedblleft{}office,\textquotedblright{} and which two earlier words wear it? (\textbf{The \emph{ma-} place shape} — \emph{madhhab} and \emph{masʾala}.) Which two earlier words share \emph{kātib}'s doer shape? (\emph{\textbf{Qāʾil}} and \emph{\textbf{qāriʾ}}.) What single letter turns an office into a library? (\textbf{\ar{ة}}.) Which English word comes from this root? (\textbf{None} — but \textbf{ketubah} comes from its Hebrew twin \emph{katav}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
